analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for employers and job agencies to screen out applicants because they are unemployed.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it an unlawful hiring practice for employers with 15 or more employees to refuse to consider, refuse to hire, or advertise jobs as closed to people who are unemployed or were unemployed in the past. Job agencies and websites that post job ads would face the same rules. Jobless workers could sue for lost wages, doubled as liquidated damages, plus attorney fees, and the Labor Department could investigate complaints and sue violators. The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed workers, especially the long-term unemployed, who during the recovery after the 2008 recession were widely screened out of hiring pools. They would gain a legal right to have their applications considered and a way to sue when rejected solely for their unemployment status.

how_it_helps.text: Bars employers with 15 or more employees from refusing to consider or hire someone because they are currently or were previously unemployed, and from running job ads stating that unemployed people need not apply.
Applies the same bans to employment agencies and to websites that publish job ads, so unemployed applicants cannot be filtered out at the screening or referral stage.

Lets affected workers sue in federal or state court for lost wages and benefits, plus an equal amount in liquidated damages, attorney fees, and in some cases punitive damages, with a two-year deadline (three for willful violations).
Directs the Secretary of Labor to receive, investigate, and try to resolve complaints and allows the Department to sue violators and pay recovered sums directly to affected workers.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers and staffing or recruiting firms that use unemployment status as a screening shortcut would face lawsuits, damages, and compliance costs. Recruiters would need to document that hiring decisions rest on job-related qualifications rather than employment gaps.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new private right of action with liquidated damages doubling any award, which exposes employers to litigation over hiring decisions and would push some to document or defend screening practices more heavily; the text itself allows courts to impose a $1,000-per-day penalty in place of lost wages.

Screening on unemployment duration is sometimes a stand-in for skills employers believe erode over time, so a blanket ban forces hiring decisions to be justified on other grounds even where the connection to job performance is disputed; the bill only carves out cases where recent similar employment is a bona fide occupational qualification.
The remedies cover lost wages tied to a specific job, so they cannot fully make jobless workers whole for the cumulative cost of being filtered out of hiring pools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For jobless workers in a slow-hiring economy, the benefit of being legally entitled to a fair look at their application is real, and the 2009-2011 recovery made unemployment-based screening a widely discussed barrier. The main cost falls on employers and recruiters as new litigation and compliance exposure, and the doubling of damages is aggressive. On balance the bill would have shifted hiring practices toward considering the jobless, which its authors argued also reduced unemployment insurance and welfare burdens.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the Fair Employment Opportunity Act of 2011 on July 12, 2011, with 28 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and on September 8, 2011 to that committee's Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions subcommittee.
All 48 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or consideration on the House floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and staffing firms that screen applicants by unemployment status are better off because the bill died; they never faced the new damages liability or advertising restrictions. Jobless workers got no federal protection, and states kept bearing the unemployment insurance and public-assistance costs the bill's findings described.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and recruiters who screen out the jobless

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar hiring discrimination against unemployed people.

for.name: 48 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, sent it to a subcommittee on September 8, 2011, and never scheduled a hearing or markup in the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee's agenda and never brought the bill to a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: the sponsor and all 48 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored. The bill died in the Republican-chaired committee without a vote, so the split, while never tested on a roll call, followed party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away their ability to filter out unemployed applicants and exposed them to suits for lost wages doubled as liquidated damages. Because the bill died, they keep the screening practice at no cost; their interest in avoiding lawsuits ran against jobless workers' interest in consideration.
Agencies could no longer refuse to consider or refer unemployed candidates, or classify them to limit their access to job listings. The bill's failure leaves their screening discretion intact.

The bill explicitly covered websites that publish job ads, barring them from hosting listings that exclude the unemployed, but also defined them as covered 'employment agencies,' creating direct liability. The bill died, so no change took effect.
